A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.
Problem 351. Quorum and majority in a 19-member committee
Voting rules often contain more than one threshold. Quorum concerns participation; majority concerns the votes cast according to the stated rule.

A committee has 19 members. 19 are present. Votes: yes=9, no=9, abstain=1. Rule: quorum is at least 60% of all members; if quorum exists, a motion passes when yes votes are strictly more than no votes.
First test quorum using all members as the denominator. Only then compare yes and no; abstentions count for presence but not as no votes under this rule.
Is quorum met, and does the motion pass?
1. Quorum threshold=ceil(0.60×19)=12. 2. Present=19, so quorum is met. 3. Yes=9, no=9; yes>no is False. 4. Combine the two tests.
Quorum is met; the motion does not pass.
Procedural reasoning requires applying tests in the right order and using the correct denominator.
Threshold predicates: quorum(present,total) and majority(yes,no); pass = quorum ∧ majority.

Representation can be modeled by rules that convert population into seats. Different allocation rules can produce different results, so the rule must be stated.

Three districts have populations A=120, B=100, C=60. They must share 12 seats. Use this stated method: compute each exact quota population/total×seats; give each district the whole-number part; assign remaining seats to the largest fractional remainders.
Use only the stated largest-remainder method. Seat totals must add exactly to the available number.
How many seats does each district receive?

1. Total population=280. 2. Exact quotas: A=5.14, B=4.29, C=2.57. 3. Initial whole seats: [5, 4, 2], leaving 1. 4. Give the remaining seat(s) to the largest remainder(s). 5. Final allocation=[5, 4, 3], which sums to 12.
Fair representation is not just arithmetic; it depends on an explicit apportionment procedure.
Largest-remainder apportionment: quotas, floors, then rank fractional remainders.

Problem 361. Which institution has the role? Repair a broken public road
Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should repair a broken public road.
Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar.
